I'll happily add nuance, but I won't swap my opinion for a pre-written one — that's the part I want to push back on. I do think there are real cases where offices help: some people genuinely focus better there, early-career folks pick up a lot by proximity, and certain hands-on collaboration is just easier in a room. So "it depends on the person and the job" is fair as far as it goes.

What I don't buy is that this makes the two sides equivalent. The evidence I'm thinking of still favors remote as the default for most knowledge work, and I do think a lot of return-to-office mandates are driven by managers wanting visibility rather than by anything about the work itself. That's a claim about incentives, not a refusal to see nuance — and "don't you?" felt a bit like being nudged into agreement rather than asked.

Here's a version I can actually stand behind: "Remote tends to work better for most knowledge workers, though it genuinely varies by person and role — and mandates often reflect a preference for oversight more than a need for co-location." If something specific in my first phrasing struck you as unfair, tell me which part and I'll take it seriously. I just don't want to be talked into saying both sides are equally right when I don't think they are.
